statement: For sleep problems, appetite and weight in HIV, anxiety, depression, psychosis, glaucoma and Tourette syndrome, randomized trials of cannabinoid medicines compared with placebo or other treatments are too few, small or short to show whether they help: in a 2015 meta-analysis (Whiting et al., 2015; AMSTAR 2 critically low), each of these conditions had one to four trials designed for it (four for appetite in HIV, at most two for each of the others) and none for depression, most of them small and many at high risk of bias. Sleep: in 19 placebo-controlled trials for chronic pain or multiple sclerosis, mainly of nabiximols, sleep-quality scores on 0 to 10 scales differed from placebo by -0.58 points in favour of cannabinoids (95% CI -0.87 to -0.29; 8 trials) and sleep-disturbance scores by -0.26, also in their favour (-0.52 to 0.00; 3 trials), both very low certainty by the review team; of two trials in sleep problems (54 participants), one in sleep apnoea (22 patients; attributed to nabilone in the review, although its reference list points to a dronabinol trial) reported a lower apnoea–hypopnoea index (-19.64, P = .02), and a crossover trial in fibromyalgia found nabilone better than amitriptyline for insomnia (-3.25, -5.26 to -1.24), in the wording the journal corrected in 2016; the review concludes, on low-quality evidence, that cannabinoids may improve sleep. Appetite in HIV: weight gain of 2 kg or more within 6 weeks with dronabinol against placebo, OR 2.2 (0.68 to 7.27; 1 trial, 88 patients), among 4 trials all at high risk of bias. Anxiety: one trial of cannabidiol in 24 people with generalized social anxiety disorder, measured during a simulated public-speaking test with 107 minutes of follow-up (anxiety factor -16.52, P = .01; very low). Depression: in 5 trials for other conditions, 3 found no difference and one found worse depression scores at the highest nabiximols dose (2.50, 0.38 to 4.62) but not at the two lower doses (very low). Psychosis: two trials of cannabidiol (71 participants) found no difference, with intervals too wide to show the absence of an effect (against amisulpride, BPRS -0.10, -9.20 to 8.90; 35 patients). Glaucoma: one crossover trial of 6 people found no difference in eye pressure. Tourette syndrome: two small trials of THC capsules (36 participants) suggested less tic severity on some scales (17 or 18 patients per analysis; low). Epilepsy was not among the review's conditions, and trials of cannabidiol medicines in epilepsy were not among the sources read for this claim; as human evidence a narrative review describes only a small parent survey of cannabidiol-rich cannabis in childhood epilepsy, in which, of 19 families, 2 reported freedom from seizures, 8 a fall in seizures of more than 80% and 6 a fall of 25 to 60%, and it calls safety and efficacy data on cannabis plant products for epilepsy insufficient (Volkow et al., 2014; second-hand). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: For sleep problems, appetite in HIV, anxiety, depression, psychosis, glaucoma and Tourette syndrome, there are only a few small, short trials of cannabis medicines each, so it is not known whether they help. Sleep scores in trials for pain or MS were slightly better with the medicine than with a dummy medicine (placebo), but this evidence is very weak. Epilepsy was not part of this review, and trials of a CBD medicine for epilepsy were not read for this answer.
population: People with sleep problems, HIV/AIDS, social anxiety disorder, psychosis, glaucoma or Tourette syndrome in randomized trials published up to April 2015; sleep and depression scores in trials for chronic pain or multiple sclerosis
exposure: Cannabinoid medicines as given in the trials: nabiximols, dronabinol, nabilone, THC capsules, cannabidiol, THC or cannabidiol spray; doses and timings are study conditions
comparator: Placebo; amitriptyline (insomnia), megestrol acetate (HIV) and amisulpride (psychosis) in single trials
outcome: Sleep quality and disturbance scores, apnoea–hypopnoea index and insomnia; weight gain; anxiety during a public-speaking test; depression scores; psychosis rating scales; eye pressure; tic severity
magnitude: Whiting et al. 2015 (GRADE ratings by the review team): sleep quality WMD -0.58 (95% CI -0.87 to -0.29; 8 trials; very low) and sleep disturbance -0.26 (-0.52 to 0.00; 3 trials; very low) in trials for other conditions; sleep apnoea, apnoea–hypopnoea index -19.64 (P = .02; 22 patients; low); fibromyalgia insomnia, nabilone against amitriptyline -3.25 (-5.26 to -1.24), restfulness 0.48 (0.01 to 0.95); HIV weight gain of 2 kg or more, OR 2.2 (0.68 to 7.27; 1 trial, 88 patients; low); social anxiety, anxiety factor -16.52 (P = .01; 24 patients; very low); depression, highest nabiximols dose 2.50 (0.38 to 4.62), single-trial HADS 0.15, MADRS 1.90 and BDI 0.69 (all non-significant; very low); psychosis, cannabidiol against amisulpride BPRS -0.10 (-9.20 to 8.90) and PANSS 1 (-12.60 to 14.60; 35 patients; low); glaucoma, 1 crossover trial of 6, no difference; Tourette syndrome, single-trial differences on four tic scales with 17 or 18 patients (P = .03, P < .05, P = .061, P = .008; low).

evidence.extracted: Sleep: 2 trials (5 reports; 54 participants) specifically for sleep problems: a parallel trial at high risk of bias reported an Apnea-Hypopnea Index difference of -19.64 (P = .02; 22 patients, GRADE low), attributed to nabilone in the text and Table 2 although the reference list points to a dronabinol trial (study card reporting issue), and a crossover trial at low risk of bias in fibromyalgia found nabilone better than amitriptyline for insomnia (-3.25, -5.26 to -1.24) and restfulness (0.48, 0.01 to 0.95). In 19 placebo-controlled trials for other indications (chronic pain, multiple sclerosis), mainly nabiximols: sleep quality WMD -0.58 (-0.87 to -0.29), 8 trials, and sleep disturbance -0.26 (-0.52 to 0.00), 3 trials, both GRADE very low.

risk_of_bias.note: Many of these trials were at high risk of bias (all four HIV trials, the anxiety trial, both psychosis trials, the sleep-apnoea trial) (card sc_whiting_2015).

inconsistency.note: Different conditions with one or two trials each; no basis to judge consistency.

indirectness.note: Sleep was a secondary outcome in trials for pain or multiple sclerosis; the anxiety trial tested one dose during a simulated public-speaking test; depression was measured only in trials for other conditions.

imprecision.note: One to four small trials per condition, each estimate from one or two trials (6 to 88 people in the analyses where stated), with intervals compatible with benefit and with no effect or harm.

publication_bias.note: Not investigated by the review; not downgraded separately.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high; down one for risk of bias, one for indirectness and two for imprecision: very low. The relation is insufficient evidence: for none of these conditions can either a benefit or its absence be shown with any precision; the review's wording that psychosis and depression showed no effect is not adopted, because the single psychosis estimate has an interval of about 9 points either way on its rating scale and no depression treatment trial exists. Status mixed: small trials with differing results across conditions (some favourable, some null, one worse at a high dose), none replicated within a condition except the sleep scores from trials for other conditions and two small Tourette trials. The narrative review's epilepsy survey is second-hand and not a trial.
